claims.text: The target materials are multicomponent high-entropy alloys in near-equilibrium solid states just below melting.
Enhanced-sampling free-energy integration can directly compute the free-energy difference associated with fusion.
Metadynamics or parallel tempering can be implemented within atomistic simulations for this purpose.
The method can operate from the near-melting solid regime through the liquid regime.
The method is applicable across a wide range of HEA compositions.
The calculated free-energy landscape captures atomic rearrangements and configurational contributions in multicomponent alloys.
Enhanced sampling efficiently overcomes energy barriers.
Enhanced sampling captures rare events relevant to melting.
Free-energy calculations can be used to derive finite-temperature thermodynamic properties of HEAs.
The proposed calculations will accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change on melting from first principles.
The proposed calculations will accurately determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Atomistic simulations can reproduce aspects of high-temperature structural evolution and melting behavior in an HEA nanoparticle.
Prediction errors could be below 5% relative to experimental DSC data.
Traditional DSC and standard molecular dynamics lack sufficient combined accuracy, efficiency, or compositional breadth for the full complexity of HEAs.
The vast HEA compositional space creates a need for efficient exploration tools.
Applicability depends on whether sufficient configurational sampling is computationally feasible.
Extremely complex compositions may exceed current computational resources and require methodological scaling.
Quantitative errors and efficiency gains remain uncertain and will depend on the HEA and implementation.
Consistent deviations greater than 10% from independent experiments across multiple HEA compositions would falsify the proposed approach.
